correctness.summary: events buffer is stackalloc long[n*2] but the loop writes to index up to 4n-1 (and Build-read reads up to 4n-1), overflowing the stack buffer by 2n longs for any n>=1.
correctness.triggeringInput: n=1, xs={5}, ys1={0}, ys2={2}, plus any valid ys/res of length 2. events is stackalloc long[2], but line 133 writes events[0*2 + 1*2]=events[2] and line 134 writes events[3]; line 137 reads events[3].
correctness.rootCause: The method emits two events per input rectangle (open at xs[i], close at xs[i]+1), so it needs 4n longs, but only n*2 are allocated. Indices events[i*2 + n*2] and events[i*2 + n*2 + 1] reach 4n-1 while the allocation top is 2n-1, causing out-of-bounds stack writes and reads (undefined behavior / memory corruption).
correctness.suggestedFix: Allocate the buffer with the correct size: long* events = stackalloc long[n * 4]; (the array conceptually holds 2n events of 2 longs each).

correctness.summary: Histogram heights from long* h are truncated to int via (int)h[...] before computing area, producing wrong areas for heights outside int range even though h is a long array.
correctness.triggeringInput: n=1, h={5000000000} (5e9, a valid long). Expected area 5000000000, but (int)5000000000 wraps to 705032704, so area is computed as 705032704 and returned/written wrong.
correctness.rootCause: Line 46 casts the long height to int: int height = (int)h[stack[--top]]; then area = (long)height * width uses the already-truncated value. Heights are typed long* and may legitimately exceed Int32 range, so truncation gives an incorrect maximum-rectangle area.
correctness.suggestedFix: Keep the height as long: long height = h[stack[--top]]; long area = height * (long)width; (no int cast). Width remains int.

perf.summary: Hoist row-base indices and avoid the per-element branch on i>0 by special-casing the first row.
perf.currentCost: Inner loop recomputes i*width+j and (i-1)*width+j each iteration (two multiplies) and tests if (i>0) on every element, a branch that is taken for all rows except the first yet evaluated width*height times.
perf.proposedChange: Compute int rowBase = i*width; int prevBase = rowBase - width; once per row. Handle i==0 with a dedicated loop (just the rowAcc running sum, no vertical add) and i>=1 with a loop that always adds res[prevBase+j]. This removes the i>0 branch from the hot inner loop entirely.
perf.rationale: Eliminates width*height index multiplies (down to O(height)) and removes a width*height-count branch whose outcome is loop-invariant per row. The two resulting straight-line inner loops vectorize cleanly under Burst.
perf.risk: None; output identical. First-row loop writes res=rowAcc, subsequent rows add the row above, exactly as the original conditional did.

perf.summary: Hoist the per-row stack stackalloc out of the height loop to allocate it once.
perf.currentCost: int* stack = stackalloc int[width]; sits inside the for(i) loop. While stackalloc inside a loop in C# does not grow the frame each iteration (the frame is reserved once), placing it in-loop can defeat that guarantee depending on codegen and obscures intent; the stack contents are fully overwritten each row anyway since top resets to 0.
perf.proposedChange: Move int* stack = stackalloc int[width]; and the heights buffer init above the for(i) loop; reset int top=0; at the start of each row iteration. heights is already hoisted; do the same for stack.
perf.rationale: Guarantees a single frame reservation, removes any per-iteration stackalloc setup, and makes the working set explicit. No correctness change since each row re-initializes top=0 and only reads stack entries it wrote this row.
perf.risk: None functionally. Stack is fully rewritten per row before reads (entries pushed before popped), so hoisting is safe.

perf.summary: The interval sort uses O(n^2) selection-style swap sort; replace with an O(n log n) sort to fix the asymptotic bottleneck.
perf.currentCost: The double loop for(i){for(j=i+1..){if res[j]<res[i] swap}} is an O(n^2) sort of the intervals by start. For large n this dominates the whole routine (the merge pass is O(n)).
perf.proposedChange: Sort the n (start,end) pairs with an O(n log n) in-place sort over the pointer array — e.g. an unmanaged heapsort or introsort on indices/pairs keyed by res[k*2]. Keep it allocation-free using stackalloc/in-place swaps to respect house constraints (no managed Array.Sort).
perf.rationale: Lowers complexity from O(n^2) to O(n log n); for n in the thousands this is orders of magnitude fewer comparisons/swaps. Same final merged output since the merge step only requires intervals sorted by start.
perf.risk: Must keep the sort stable-enough only in the sense that ties by start don't change the union result (they don't, since merge takes max end). Implementing heapsort in unmanaged C# is more code/complexity; verify the pair-swap keeps start and end paired. Behavior preserved for all valid n>=1 (n==0 would read res[0] in the original too, so no new edge case).

perf.summary: Replace the inner j-1 underflow ternary with a branchless first-column special-case and hoist row base.
perf.currentCost: dp[j - 1 < 0 ? 0 : j - 1] evaluates a branch every cell of every row (width*height branches), and grid[i*width+j] recomputes i*width+j per cell. For j==0 the expression dp[0] is also semantically a corner the loop handles awkwardly.
perf.proposedChange: Hoist long* row = grid + i*width; (or int rowBase). Handle j==0 outside the inner loop (left neighbor contributes 0), then loop j=1..width-1 using dp[j-1] directly with no bounds ternary. Use a branchless min via Math.Min already present; the key is removing the j-1<0 test.
perf.rationale: Removes width*height branch evaluations from the hot loop and O(width*height) index multiplies (down to O(height)), tightening the dependency chain and helping Burst vectorize the steady-state inner loop.
perf.risk: Must preserve the j==0 case exactly: original uses dp[max(0,j-1)]=dp[0] when j==0, i.e. it reads dp[0] (the cell itself's previous value via temp logic). Carefully reproduce: at j==0 the min is over (dp[0]_old, dp[0]_old, prev=0) -> result is 1 when grid==1 (since prev starts 0). Reproduce that as dp[0] = grid==1 ? 1 : 0. Verify against original before applying.
